title: Why long agent runs fail
subtitle: Diagnosing agent drift as working-memory overflow, and building the control plane that holds the state instead

stats.label: work orders run under the control plane

lede: Every long autonomous coding run I launched failed the same way. Somewhere past a horizon the lead agent lost a rule, a plan step or a teammate's state, and the work quietly diverged from what had been agreed. The common response is a longer, sterner prompt. I had done that, and it bought a few more hours before the same drift returned. So I named the failure for what it is, working-memory overflow, and built the control plane that follows from that name. AgentOS moves the state out of the model and into a database, makes every job small and freshly rendered, and enforces the rules with machinery.
quote: If drift is memory overflow, the cure is less to remember.
evidence: Agent orchestration: a PostgreSQL work graph holds every work order, task, decision and cost, and each agent gets a small contract-bound job rendered at dispatch, across 246 work orders.

Diagnosing LLM agent drift: long-run failures named as working-memory overflow and answered by moving state out of the model, with recovery that rebuilds an agent's picture from the graph after a crash or compaction.
Multi-agent governance: 106 hook modules across eleven lifecycle events turn policy into refusals, so the lead agent cannot re-type or edit an artifact.
Control-plane and state-machine architecture: a Rust control plane of about 546,000 lines with 79 forward-only migrations, where 45,097 state transitions each left a receipt.
Cost attribution for AI work: 31,811 metered usage entries tied to the work that spent them.
author: Corey James
